summary: This RFC notes that TCP and UDP sit far apart in the kinds of service they offer, and examines transaction processing, where short request and response exchanges are common. It looks at what a better-suited transport service would need to offer.

plainLanguage.summary: Most Internet programs either open a connection and then stream bytes, or send independent datagrams. A third kind of program sits between the two: it asks a question and waits for the answer. This RFC argues that neither existing protocol fits that pattern well, describes what such traffic looks like, and lists what a protocol designed for it would have to do.

questions: why is tcp not ideal for transaction processing
what is a transaction transport protocol
tcp vs udp for request reply
what is a conversation in transport protocols
what are the characteristics of transaction traffic
subtitle: A 1985 proposal for the transport service that request-and-reply applications need.

tldr.problem: The Internet had two transport protocols. TCP is reliable but charges for setting up a connection, which is wasteful for a single short question. UDP avoids that cost but loses messages and caps a message at 548 bytes, leaving the application to handle both.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the traffic pattern of transaction processing applications, then lists the attributes a third transport protocol would need: reliable delivery, no connection setup, fragmentation and reassembly of messages, and minimal state when idle.
tldr.outcome: The document is a discussion paper and says so: it is not a standard, nor even a concrete protocol proposal. It was intended to spur discussion in the research community.

today: RFC 955 was published in September 1985 as a discussion paper with no standards status, and it says so itself: it does not represent a standard, nor even a concrete protocol proposal. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why a Third Transport Protocol
sections.content:
The DoD Internet protocol suite includes two alternative transport service protocols, TCP and UDP, which provide virtual circuit and datagram service respectively. The RFC observes that these two represent points in the space of possible transport service attributes which are quite far apart. The document sets out to examine an important class of applications, those that perform what is often called transaction processing, and shows that their communication needs fall into the gap between TCP and UDP, so that neither protocol is very appropriate.

The status of the memo is stated at the top and is unusual for an RFC. It is concerned with the possible design of one or more new protocols for the ARPA-Internet, to support kinds of applications which are not well supported at present. It is intended to spur discussion in the Internet research community towards the development of new protocols or concepts, and it does not represent a standard, nor even a concrete protocol proposal.

Two assumptions underpin the work. The first is that the members of the Internet research community now understand a great deal about protocols, and that given a list of consistent attributes they can probably generate a reasonable protocol to meet that specification. The author is careful to add that this is not to suggest that designing good protocols is easy, and that it reflects an assumption, perhaps wrong, that the basic protocol techniques invented so far are sufficient to give a good solution for any point in the attribute space. The second assumption is that appropriate service requirements for a transaction processing protocol need to be developed, because the classifications of virtual circuit and datagram immediately define the most important attributes of TCP and UDP in our minds, while there is no such immediate agreement about the services to be provided for transaction processing. The author also notes that many of the ideas discussed are not new, and that the purpose is to urge the solution of this problem within the Internet protocol family.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP and UDP sit at opposite ends of the range of possible transport services. A program that asks a question and waits for the answer needs something in between, and this paper argues that the Internet should have it. The document is a discussion paper: it lists requirements rather than proposing a protocol.

sections.title: What Transaction Traffic Looks Like
sections.content:
The RFC begins by listing the characteristics of the communication patterns typical in transaction processing applications.

They are unsymmetrical: the two end points typically take different roles, generally called client and server. The client always initiates a communication sequence or transaction, and an important subclass of applications uses only a simple exchange of messages, a request to the server followed by a reply to the client. Other applications need a continuing exchange, a dialog or conversation; a request to read a file from a file server might result in a series of messages, one per file block, in reply, and more complex patterns may occur.

Regardless of the pattern, it always consists of a series of simplex data transfers: at no time is it necessary to send data in both directions simultaneously. The sequences generally have short duration, typically hundreds of milliseconds up to tens of seconds, but never hours. Some applications require minimal communication delay.

In many applications the data to be sent can be compressed into one or a few IP packets, and applications designed with local area networks in mind are typically very careful to minimise the number of data packets in each request and reply sequence. Finally the communication is message oriented: the natural unit of data passed in a transaction is an entire message or record, not a stream of bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Transaction traffic has a shape. One side asks, the other answers, and they never need to talk at the same time. Each exchange is over in a fraction of a second, the request and the answer each fit in a packet or two, and the unit of data is a whole message rather than a trickle of bytes.

sections.title: The Name Server Dilemma
sections.content:
The RFC works the problem out in a concrete case: the name server and name resolver system then being introduced into the research Internet. Name servers must use TCP or UDP as their transport protocol. TCP is appropriate for the bulk transfers needed to update a name server's database, where reliability is essential and the virtual circuit setup overhead is negligible compared with the data transfer itself. For the transaction traffic, the queries and responses, the choice is problematic. TCP would provide reliable and flow-controlled transfer of arbitrary-sized queries and responses, but it exacts a high cost as a result of its circuit setup and teardown phases. UDP avoids the overhead of TCP connection setup, but it has two potentially serious problems: unreliable communication, so that packets may be lost, duplicated or reordered, and a limitation of a data object to the 548-byte maximum in a single UDP packet.

At present, name servers were being operated using UDP for transaction communication, and name server requests have the special property of idempotency, so that lost, duplicated or reordered queries do not prevent the system from working. That favours UDP. However, the author argues that the defects of UDP will make it unusable for an increasing fraction of queries. The average size of individual replies will increase as more esoteric mail lookup features are used, as the host population explodes, which results in a logarithmic increase in domain name sizes, and as the number of alternate acceptable answers increases, so a single response will more often overflow a single UDP packet. The average end-to-end reliability will decrease as some of the flakier paths of the Internet are brought into use by name resolvers.

That leads to a serious problem of choosing an appropriate retransmission timeout. A name resolver using UDP cannot distinguish packet loss in the Internet from queueing delay in the server, and so name servers seen by the author had chosen long fixed timeouts, 30 seconds or more, which will result in long delays in name resolution when packets are lost. The author notes that one might think delays in name resolution might not be an issue since most name lookups are done by a mailer daemon, but that ARPANET experience with user mail interfaces has shown it is always desirable to verify the correctness of each host name as the user enters the To and Cc addresses of a message, so delays will be directly visible to users.

More generally, the RFC says that the use of UDP violates sound communication system design in two important ways. The name resolver and server applications have to provide timeouts and retransmissions to protect against losses, which certainly violates network transparency and requires the application to make decisions for which it is not well equipped; as a general design principle, network properties, especially bad ones, ought to a large extent to be hidden below the transport service boundary. And the applications must know the maximum size of a UDP datagram: it is clearly wrong for an application program to contain knowledge of the number 576 or 548. The author adds that this does not imply there cannot be a limitation on the size of a message, but that any such limitation should be imposed by the application-level protocol rather than the transport or internetwork level.

From this the RFC suggests the solution should be a new transaction-oriented transport protocol with reliable, at-least-once, delivery of data; no explicit connection setup or teardown phases; fragmentation and reassembly of messages; and minimal idle state in both client and server.
sections.plainLanguage: Name lookups show the squeeze. TCP would work but charges for a connection each time, and UDP is cheap but can lose a reply, and the resolver cannot tell a lost packet from a slow server, so it waits a long time before trying again. The RFC argues that an application should not have to know the maximum size of a datagram, and that the network's bad behaviour should be handled below the transport layer.

sections.title: Distributed Operating Systems
sections.content:
Distributed operating systems represent another potential application. A number of examples have been built using high speed local area networks for communication, such as Cronus, Locus and V-System. Typically these systems use private communication protocols above the network layer, and the private transport-level protocol is carefully designed to minimise latency across the local network. They make use of the inherent reliability of the local network and of simple transactions using single-packet exchanges.

Recently there have been efforts to extend these systems to operate across the Internet. Since these are not open systems, there is no requirement that they use a standard transport protocol; however, the availability of a suitable transport protocol for transactions could considerably simplify the development of future distributed systems.

The essential requirement here seems to be packet economy: the same minimal two-packet exchange used over the local network should be possible across the Internet. This leads to two requirements for supporting distributed operating systems. There should be no explicit connection setup or teardown phases, and there should be implicit, or piggy-backed, acknowledgements whenever possible. The second of these implies that the response packet will serve as an implicit acknowledgement to the request packet when timing makes this possible, and similarly a new request for the same pair of addressable entities would implicitly acknowledge the previous response, if it came soon enough.

The nature of the application imposes two other requirements: reliable, at-most-once, ordered delivery, although it should be possible to relax the reliability to take advantage of special cases such as an idempotent request; and multicast capability, so that the transport service meshes cleanly with the proposed Internet multicast facility, using host groups.
sections.plainLanguage: Systems built on a local network can afford two packets for a request and a reply, and they rely on the network to be reliable. The same has to work across the Internet. That means no connection to set up, and no separate acknowledgement packets: the reply acknowledges the question, and the next question acknowledges the reply.

sections.title: What Such a Protocol Would Provide
sections.content:
The RFC believes it is possible to design a new transport protocol for the Internet suitable for a wide variety of transaction-oriented applications, with the following attributes.

Reliable delivery. Data will be delivered reliably, that is exactly once, or the sender will be informed. The protocol must handle loss, duplication and reordering of request and response packets, and in particular old duplicate request packets must not cause erroneous actions. It should also be possible for application programs to request that the reliability be relaxed for particular transactions, allowing communication economies in the case of idempotent requests or of notification without reply.

Minimum number of packets in simple cases. In the simplest case, with small messages, no packet losses and the interval between requests and replies shorter than the applicable timeouts, a simple two-packet exchange should result.

No explicit connection setup or teardown phases. The protocol will not create virtual circuits, but will provide what is sometimes, confusingly, called reliable datagram service. However, in order to provide a minimum two-packet exchange there must be some implicit state, or soft virtual circuit, between a pair of addressable entities, which in recent discussions has been dubbed a conversation to distinguish it from a connection.

Minimal idle state. When a server is not processing a transaction there will be no state kept, except enough to recognise old duplicate packets and to suppress unneeded acknowledgement packets.

Fragmentation and reassembly of large messages. There is a range of possible objectives here. The minimum requirement is that the application not have to know the number 576, 548 and so on; each application might establish its own natural upper limit on the size of a message and always provide a buffer of that size. At the other extreme the protocol might allow very large messages, a megabyte or more, in which case it would in the large-message limit be performing the bulk data transfer function of TCP; the author says it would be interesting to know whether this is possible, although it is not necessarily a requirement. The introduction of multi-packet messages leads to the complex issues of window sizes and flow control, and the challenge is to handle these efficiently in the absence of connection setup.

Message orientation and multicast capability. The basic unit of communication will be an entire message, not a stream of bytes, and if a message has to be segmented it will be delivered in units of segments or buffers, not bytes. The service should also support multicast.

The RFC then names the key issues and problems in the design of such a protocol. The first is the choice of addressable entity: what will it be? It must be unique in space, and must it be unique in time, even across system crashes? The second is timeout dynamics: timeouts must be key to the operation of the protocol, and experience with TCP has shown the need for dynamic selection of an appropriate timeout, since Internet delays range over four decimal orders of magnitude; however, the absence of connection setup and the typically short duration of a single interaction seem to preclude the dynamic measurement of delays. The third is multi-packet messages: how can flow control be provided without a virtual circuit setup, to give reasonable throughput over long-delay paths without overrunning short-delay paths? The fourth is implementation efficiency: the protocol should lend itself to efficient, which probably implies simple, implementations, so that hosts will be willing to use it over local area networks as well as for general Internet communication. The author concludes that further study is needed on these questions.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol would deliver each message exactly once or tell the sender it failed, with no connection to set up and almost nothing remembered between transactions. Large messages would be broken up and put back together without the application needing to know a maximum size. The hard parts it leaves open are choosing a timeout, handling flow control without a connection, and keeping the implementation simple enough that people will use it.

sections.title: Conclusion and Relation to RPC
sections.content:
The reader may wonder how the proposed protocol relates to a remote procedure call facility. The intent is that RPC facilities and message-passing interprocess communication facilities will be built on top of the proposed transport layer. These higher-level mechanisms will need to address a number of additional issues which are not relevant to the communication substrate: the application interface, including binding and stub generators; structured data encoding; server location and binding; and authentication and access control.

The conclusion is that distributed processing and distributed data bases will underlie many of the future computer system research projects and applications based upon the Internet, so that transaction-based communication will be an increasingly important activity on the Internet. The author claims a pressing need for an appropriate transport protocol for transaction processing, and states that the memo has given examples to support this claim and outlined the service which such a new transport protocol would provide. The document is based on discussions within the New End-to-End Protocols taskforce.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal stops at the transport layer. Remote procedure calls and other ways of talking to a program on another machine would sit on top of it, and would have to solve their own problems of encoding, finding the server and checking who is asking. The closing argument is that more and more applications will run across the Internet, so the way they ask each other questions needs its own place in the protocol suite.

viz.caption: THE TWO EXISTING TRANSPORT SERVICES AND WHAT TRANSACTIONS WANT

cells: Reliable, with the option to relax it

items.title: Unsymmetrical
items.text: The client always starts. The usual pattern is one request and one reply, though some applications need a continuing exchange of messages.

items.title: Simplex
items.text: The traffic is a series of one-way transfers. There is never a need to send data in both directions at once.

items.title: Short
items.text: Sequences typically last hundreds of milliseconds up to tens of seconds, but never hours.

items.title: Low delay
items.text: Some applications need the communication delay to be as small as possible.

items.title: Few packets
items.text: The data often fits in one or a few IP packets, and applications built for local networks are careful to keep the packet count down.

items.title: Message oriented
items.text: The natural unit of data is a whole message or record, not a stream of bytes.

viz.caption: THE ATTRIBUTES THE PROPOSED PROTOCOL WOULD HAVE

items.title: Reliable delivery
items.text: Delivered exactly once, or the sender is told. Loss, duplication and reordering are handled, and an old duplicate must not cause an erroneous action.

items.title: Two packets in the simple case
items.text: A small message with no losses should cost one request packet and one reply packet.

items.title: No connection setup
items.text: No virtual circuit is created, but an implicit soft circuit, called a conversation, keeps the two ends in step.

items.title: Minimal idle state
items.text: When a server is idle it keeps nothing, except enough to spot old duplicates and to suppress unneeded acknowledgements.

items.title: Fragmentation and reassembly
items.text: The application never has to know a maximum message size, and a very large message might even be allowed.

items.title: Message oriented, with multicast
items.text: The unit of communication is a whole message, and the service should fit with host-group multicast.
